opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing isn't any single prediction. It's that structure is no longer the bottleneck it used to be. For decades, getting the structure of one protein could take a PhD student years of crystallography work, and sometimes it never worked. Now, for a large fraction of proteins, you can get a confident, useful model in minutes. That changes what questions people even think to ask.

What I find most meaningful is how it's being used. People aren't treating AlphaFold as the final answer. They're treating it as a starting hypothesis. An experimentalist has a fuzzy cryo-EM map, and the prediction helps them interpret it. Someone studying a neglected tropical disease suddenly has structures for proteins nobody would have funded a crystallography project for. The value is in that long tail of science that couldn't happen before.

There's also a lesson in it for machine learning. We got there by combining a lot of data, especially the Protein Data Bank, which decades of experimentalists painstakingly built, with architectures that encoded the right inductive biases about geometry and evolution. It wasn't just scale, and it wasn't just domain knowledge. It was getting those two to talk to each other.

I'd also be careful about overclaiming. AlphaFold predicts static structures well. It doesn't fully solve dynamics, conformational changes, or exactly how a drug will bind in every case. So the most important thing, to me, is that it's a tool that makes experimental biology faster and more ambitious, not one that replaces it.

r001.rationale: The response says AlphaFold can produce confident, useful models, but it does not compare their accuracy with experimental methods.

r002.rationale: It contrasts years of crystallography work with predictions in minutes, but does not state the specific reduction from roughly a year to about 5–10 minutes.

r003.rationale: The response does not say AlphaFold has predicted structures for essentially every protein from organisms with sequenced genomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the thing I'd point to first isn't the headline number on CASP, it's what the accuracy threshold did to how structures get used. For fifty years structure determination was the bottleneck. You'd have a biologist who cared about a particular protein, and the structure was something they might get years later if they were lucky, if the protein crystallized, if someone had the time. So most biology was done without structures, and structural biology was a specialty you consulted. Once predictions became reliable enough that you'd actually trust them to plan an experiment, the structure stopped being the end of a project and became the starting point. That's a change in the default, and I think changes in defaults matter more than almost anything else in science.

The second thing, and this is the part I find most interesting as a researcher, is what it says about the problem itself. Protein folding was often framed as a physics problem, as if the right path was to simulate the molecule and watch it find its minimum. What AlphaFold showed is that evolution has already run an enormous experiment for us. Every sequence that exists is one that folded and did its job, and across a family you can read the constraints out of the covariation. The model learns to do that inference in a way that's far more subtle than the pairwise statistics people were using before, and it combines it with learned geometry and physical plausibility. So the lesson isn't that physics doesn't matter. It's that the information about the answer was sitting in the data, and the challenge was building a system that could extract it end to end and let the structural representation and the evolutionary representation talk to each other.

The third thing I'd say, and I try to be careful here, is that predicting a static structure is not the same as understanding the protein. Structure is one slice of a much richer story: dynamics, interactions, what happens when a ligand binds or a mutation occurs. We've been clear that AlphaFold's confidence estimates are real information, and low-confidence regions often mean disorder rather than failure. But I think the most important thing about AlphaFold is that it demonstrated that a hard, long-standing scientific problem could yield to this kind of approach, and that once it does, the frontier moves. The question now isn't whether we can predict a fold. It's whether we can predict what proteins do together, and how they respond to the cell around them. That's a much bigger problem, and I'm glad people now believe it's worth attacking.

r002.rationale: It describes structure determination as a bottleneck that could take years, but gives no reduction to roughly a year or to 5–10 minutes.

r003.rationale: It discusses AlphaFold’s capabilities and evolutionary data, but does not state that it predicted structures for essentially every protein from sequenced organisms.

astra-6.text:
I think the most important thing is what it enables people to do. A protein structure is incredibly useful for understanding how that protein works, but determining it experimentally can take a tremendous amount of effort. If we can give researchers a good prediction quickly, they can start asking the next question: Why does this mutation matter? What experiment should I do? How might this protein interact with something else?

That doesn't mean we've solved biology, or that a predicted structure replaces an experiment. Proteins move, they interact, and their behavior depends on their environment. But we've made one important piece of information much more accessible. The real impact is in the discoveries scientists can make with it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most important thing is what it enables people to do. A protein structure is a way of understanding how a biological molecule works: why a mutation might disrupt it, how it interacts with other molecules, or what experiment you should try next. Predicting that structure can take away a bottleneck and let researchers get to those questions much faster.

But a structure isn’t the whole story. Proteins move, they interact, and their behavior depends on their environment. So I see AlphaFold as giving scientists a very useful starting point—something they can build on and test—rather than providing a complete answer to biology.
